planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in low to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Janet Craig tolerates dimmer interior corners better than most other dracaena cultivars.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in low to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix. Janet Craig is one of the oldest and most enduring dracaena cultivars, prized for its solid, glossy, deep green, broad strap-like leaves and its exceptional tolerance of dim interior light, making it a mainstay of offices, lobbies, and other low-window spaces where more colorful dracaenas fade. It grows slowly into an upright, cane-forming plant that can be kept as a single trunk or trained multi-stem, and it holds up well under fluorescent light and inconsistent watering typical of commercial interiors. Water when the top half of the potting mix dries out, avoid overwatering since this cultivar is especially prone to root rot in soggy soil, and keep it away from cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dracaena Production Guide

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in low to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Warneckii tolerates dim interior light nearly as well as Janet Craig while adding white-striped variegation.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in low to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix, historically classified as Dracaena deremensis 'Warneckii' before that species was folded into Dracaena fragrans. Warneckii carries long, narrow, arching leaves striped lengthwise in gray-green with crisp white to pale silvery margins, giving it a cooler, more silvery presence than the solid dark green of Janet Craig while sharing the same tough constitution. It forms a dense, bushy, multi-caned clump rather than a single tall cane, making it useful as a floor plant that fills space at eye level, and it is one of the more forgiving dracaenas for offices and other rooms with only moderate window light. Water when the top half of the potting mix dries, avoid soggy soil to prevent root rot, and keep away from temperatures below 55°F.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dracaena Production Guide

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in low to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Compacta's dense rosette habit suits tabletops and shelves better than the taller straight species.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in low to bright indirect light in well-drained potting mix. Compacta is a dwarf sport of the common corn plant, forming tight, dense rosettes of short, glossy, dark green leaves on a slow-growing cane rather than the tall, loosely tufted canes typical of the species, which keeps it naturally small and full without pruning. Its compact rosette habit makes it well suited to tabletops, shelves, and terrariums where a full-size dracaena would quickly outgrow the space, while it retains the same tolerance for low light and inconsistent watering that makes the species so durable indoors. Water when the top half of the potting mix dries out, avoid overwatering to prevent root rot, and keep away from cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Dracaena Production Guide

planting.note: Root cut canes in plain water or plant rooted canes in well-drained potting mix in low to bright indirect light; Lucky Bamboo grown in water needs the vase topped off weekly and the water fully changed every one to two weeks to prevent stagnation.

directions: Root cut canes in plain water or plant rooted canes in well-drained potting mix in low to bright indirect light, avoiding direct sun which scorches the thin leaves. Despite its common name, Lucky Bamboo is not a true bamboo at all but a slender-stemmed dracaena, sold as straight canes, spirals, or braided stems that are often trained into decorative shapes while young and stay that way as they mature. It is exceptionally tolerant of low light and neglect, making it a popular desk and tabletop plant, though canes grown long-term in water alone benefit from a diluted liquid fertilizer occasionally since plain water lacks nutrients. If grown in water, use filtered or distilled water rather than tap water where possible, since this species is notably sensitive to fluoride and chlorine, which cause the leaf tips to brown. All parts are toxic to cats and dogs if ingested.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix; Song of Jamaica tolerates lower light than the variegated 'Song of India' since it carries no variegation to fade.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix. Song of Jamaica is the solid-green counterpart to the variegated Song of India, with dense whorls of narrow, glossy, deep green leaves spiraling tightly around upright, densely branching stems, giving it a fuller, bushier profile than most cane-type dracaenas. Its uniform green coloring makes it noticeably more shade-tolerant than variegated reflexa cultivars, since it has no cream or yellow pigment to fade or scorch in lower light, and it develops a naturally dense, shrubby form that needs little pruning to look full. Water when the top inch or two of potting mix dries out, avoid cold drafts and temperatures below 55°F, and rotate the pot occasionally for even, symmetrical growth.
